stem:
A 48-year-old man is evaluated for recurrent abdominal pain.  Serum levels of vitamin D and other fat-soluble vitamins are low.  Fecal levels of elastase-1 and chymotrypsin are also low.  A normal, noncontrast CT scan of the abdomen is shown in the image below.  Involvement of which of the following labeled structures is most likely causing this patient's symptoms?

​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​
explanation:
This patient with abdominal pain has fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies (eg, vitamin D) and low levels of pancreatic enzymes (eg, chymotrypsin, elastase-1).  These findings are consistent with pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, most commonly due to chronic pancreatitis.  Chronic pancreatitis results in acinar cell atrophy and fibrosis, resulting in impaired digestive enzyme synthesis and nutrient absorption.  Fecal levels of elastase-1 (which remain stable during gastrointestinal transport) and chymotrypsin are used to assess pancreatic function and confirm the diagnosis in early disease, when symptoms may be mild.

CT scan may reveal a normal-appearing pancreas in its early stages, progressing to pancreatic atrophy, ductal dilation, and calcifications.  Anatomically, the head, neck, and body of the pancreas are retroperitoneal, whereas the tail is peritoneal.  The head of the pancreas lies in the curve of the duodenum, with the body making contact posteriorly with the aorta, left adrenal gland, left kidney, and renal vessels.  The tail of the pancreas courses within the splenorenal ligament alongside the splenic vessels.

(Choices A and B)  These structures correspond to the second (descending) part of the duodenum and jejunum, respectively.  Celiac disease can present with abdominal pain and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies caused by malabsorption due to duodenal and jejunal villous atrophy in response to dietary gluten.  However, it does not impact pancreatic exocrine function; therefore, normal fecal levels of pancreatic elastase-1 and chymotrypsin are expected.

(Choice C)  This retroperitoneal structure corresponds to the right kidney.  Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease can cause flank pain (ie, renal hemorrhage), chronic kidney disease, and vitamin D deficiency due to impaired renal conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D into 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D (active form).  However, deficiencies in other fat-soluble vitamins (ie, A, E, K) and decreased fecal elastase-1 and chymotrypsin are not expected.

(Choice D)  This structure corresponds to the liver.  Cholestatic liver disease (eg, advanced primary biliary cholangitis) obstructs the secretion of bile acids into intrahepatic bile ducts, impairing dietary fat digestion and resulting in fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies.  However, pancreatic exocrine function is unaffected; therefore, decreased fecal elastase-1 and chymotrypsin levels are not expected.

Educational objective:Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (commonly caused by chronic pancreatitis) presents with fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies and low fecal pancreatic enzyme levels (eg, elastase-1, chymotrypsin).  CT findings may include a normal-appearing pancreas (identified by its proximity to the descending part of the duodenum and aorta) or may reveal atrophy, calcifications, and ductal dilations.​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​
